Uh, but generally it is a, there, there are several different variables on how a property owner can go about getting, uh, one of these exemptions or improvement, depending on the use of the property, whether it's a single family dwelling, a multiple dwelling or construction or an industrial use, uh, the statute breaks the three down, um, and you can be eligible as a property owner to receive one of the, some of those benefits by making improvements to your property, by constructing, uh, making new construction to the property or by converting, uh, one, another use of prior use to one of these three uses. So to give an example, without turning this into an hour long webinar, uh, if the property has a single family dwelling that, uh, is improved on the property and they make improvements to it, the ordinance, uh, which tracks the statute allows an exemption of up to $25,000 of the value of the improvements. So for example, if the improvements are valued by your tax assessor at $50,000, well, half of that can count as an exemption for the five-year period. Um, the town benefits because it incentivized the property owner to improve his or her property, uh, which might not otherwise happen. And it gets for at least the five-year period, uh, an increase in the assessed value of 25,000. The property owner gets the benefit of saving some tax dollars as a benefit of making an investment in his property. And in the town, uh, after that five-year period, it all results, you know, it goes away the exemption and in year six, what the taxes would be due, uh, as normal, uh, takes effect. So, uh, for, for most of the examples, whether it's a single family or multiple, uh, dwelling, uh, all the property owner would need to do is fill out the state form. There's a state, uh, there's a state form, um, and presented to the tax assessor, it's an automatic approval of those of that, uh, exemption and abatement. Uh, for some of the larger projects, the new construction, commercial, industrial, it does require council action and an agreement, uh, between the property owner and the governing body. And there's various formulas that can be used to calculate what the exemption and abatement would be. And it's really viewed in a case by case basis. Uh, but generally the most common formula that's used is what we refer to as the phase-in, uh, meaning that once you calculate what the exemption amount is going to be, uh, it phases in over that five-year period. So in year one, the property owner is going to be paying whatever the taxes were in the year prior. So the municipality doesn't lose any money plus 20% of, of the new value or the improved value in year two, it's 40%, then 60%, then 80%. And then by year six, you're paying the full amount of the assessed value of the property. Um, so that's, that's the skinny of it.
